01The network

A shared space for racialized leaders

The Racialized Executives Network brings together executives who identify with racialized communities from across the Government of Canada.

It is being established as a space for peer support, learning and collaboration. Its purpose is to support members and bring their perspectives to work on equity, representation and inclusive leadership.

The network’s planned activities

  1. Peer connection

    Share experiences, practical advice and knowledge with other racialized executives.

  2. Leadership development

    Explore professional development, mentorship and opportunities for leadership growth.

  3. Work on systemic barriers

    Discuss barriers in recruitment, career progression and workplace culture, drawing on evidence and lived experience.

  4. Representation and participation

    Bring racialized executives’ perspectives into discussions that shape the public service.

  5. Partnerships across the public service

    Work with other employee networks and government-wide equity and inclusion initiatives.

02Evidence and context

What the published data show

Representation, career progression and workplace experiences measure different things. Each view below identifies its population, period and source.

15.6%

Executive workforce availability benchmark

Racialized executive representation is 1.7 percentage points above this benchmark.

23.9%

Racialized share of the overall workforce

A workforce comparison, distinct from the executive availability benchmark.

3.2%

Black share of the executive workforce

255 Black executives. Black employees are included within the racialized total.

The executive national labour market availability estimate is 20.6%. Racialized executive representation is 3.3 percentage points below this broader benchmark. Executive WFA, at 15.6%, applies additional filters for public service occupations. These two availability measures answer different questions.

Coverage: core public administration, as of 31 March 2025. These figures do not cover every federal employer. The executive population includes the Law Management (LC) group and excludes deputy ministers and Governor in Council appointees.

The difference between these shares is a workforce comparison. It is not a workforce availability gap or an individual promotion probability.

Nine-year trend and executive availability benchmarks

Workforce availability (WFA) estimates the available talent for public service occupations. Benchmarks change when census sources, population coverage or the workforce mix change. They are not a fixed target across years. The overall executive benchmark is not a published benchmark for each individual EX level.

Different communities, different representation

The racialized total combines communities with different patterns of representation. These figures compare each subgroup’s share of all executives with its share of the overall workforce in the core public administration.

Subgroup names follow the publisher’s categories. A difference in shares does not, by itself, establish discrimination. No subgroup-specific WFA benchmark is supplied in this table.

04Career progression

Entry into executive roles and advancement within them

The PSC’s promotion study distinguishes promotions within the EX group from promotions out of EX minus 1 feeder groups. Results vary by pathway and racialized subgroup.

How to read the estimates

These are differences in model-estimated promotion rates relative to the comparison group. They are not the percentage of employees promoted, annual rates or percentage-point gaps. For racialized groups, the comparator is employees who are not members of visible minorities within the relevant career pathway.

A result without a significance marker does not establish a statistically discernible difference. The six study periods overlap. Estimates describe the study periods, which end in 2023.

Executive staffing movements in 2024–2025

The percentages are each group’s share of all executive hires, promotions or separations in that year. They are not an individual’s probability of promotion or departure. These totals do not distinguish promotions into the executive group from promotions within it. Hires and separations are payroll movements; promotions are from PSC staffing data.

05Workplace experiences

What racialized executives reported in the 2024 PSES

Compare survey responses from racialized and non-racialized executives. The survey population differs from the employment equity population above. The comparisons describe respondents’ experiences and perceptions.

Public service aggregate. Percentages use the publisher’s combined response measure. No statistical significance test is provided here.

Response options and interpretation

    Combined, positive and negative measures follow TBS definitions and may exclude “Don’t know” and “Not applicable” responses. An individual response option uses the published answer field. These percentages can have different denominators.

    The response counts are rounded counts for the question. They may include responses excluded from a combined percentage. They are not population headcounts. Suppressed or unavailable values are displayed as unavailable and are never treated as zero.

    Compare all retained questions for the selected organization
    Historical context: racialized executives in the 2022 PSES

    The 2022 executive report used “all other employees” as the comparison group. That includes non-executives and differs from the non-racialized executive comparator used in the 2024 view. These tables should not be read as a direct trend in the gap between racialized and non-racialized executives.

    06Evidence on barriers

    Representation is one part of the picture

    2 / 18

    audited employers met the horizontal audit’s requirements

    Canadian Human Rights Commission, sector-wide report published in 2025. The 18 audited organizations were selected from 46 organizations that completed a self-assessment.

    The CHRC’s audit of racialized people in management and executive positions identified barriers in recruitment, selection, hiring decisions, career development and workplace culture.

    • Among the 33 surveyed organizations that had conducted an employment systems review, 63.6% reported barriers to hiring or promoting racialized people into management or executive roles.
    • The audit found weaknesses in concrete measures, accountability and monitoring. Aggregate representation could meet availability while barriers remained.

    These are findings about the organizations and processes studied. They are not a prevalence estimate for every federal executive or a finding about an individual staffing decision.

      Membership and participation
      Who is the network for?
      The network brings together federal public service executives who identify with racialized communities. Contact the network or visit its GCXchange space for membership information.
      Can I contribute occasionally?
      You can offer help with one task or event, suggest an idea or discuss ongoing support. Use the contribution form to indicate your interests and availability.
      How do I send my contribution form?
      Complete the form and review your response. Open the prepared email, check its contents and select Send in your email application. You can also copy or download your response.
      How can I request another format?
      Use the network contact link below to report an accessibility barrier or request another format. Include the page section and the format that would work for you.

      Official sources
        Coverage, definitions and limits
        Terminology and self-identification
        This website uses “racialized” in its own text. Some source tables use “members of visible minorities,” the category used in the published employment equity data. Indigenous identity is a separate employment equity category and is not added to the racialized total. The PSES comparison group “non-racialized executives” follows the source’s definition and should not be read as “White executives.”
        Representation data depend on voluntary self-identification. Survey data depend on voluntary participation and question eligibility. Categories may overlap. Group differences alone do not establish their causes.
        Staffing survey coverage
        The 2023 and 2025 Staffing and Non-Partisanship Survey publications provide racialized employee results and occupational-group results in separate views. An executive-by-racialized intersection is not included in these tables. The executive promotion study provides separate evidence on executive career progression.
